title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone, the tutors and governesses made their bows, and they went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor stayed behind. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," answered Nicholas Bolkonski, also in a whisper.
"Ma tante, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face was full of entreaty, agitation, and ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here, he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you directly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, offering his hand to the Swiss tutor, and then he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't had a proper look at each other yet.... How he's grown to look like him, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, flushing crimson, looking up at Pierre with bright, rapturous eyes.

Pierre nodded, and went on with what he had been saying before the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat down to her woolwork; Natasha never took her eyes off her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, went to fetch more tea from Sonya, who sat weary but resolute at the samovar, and put questions to Pierre. The curly-headed, delicate boy sat unnoticed in a corner, his eyes shining, starting every now and then and muttering something under his breath, clearly caught up in some new and powerful feeling as he kept turning his curly head, with its thin neck bared by his turned-down collar, toward the place where Pierre sat.

The conversation turned to the current gossip about those in power—the subject most people find of greatest interest in domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government on account of his own disappointments in the service, listened with pleasure to the things being done in Petersburg, things that struck him as foolish, and made sharp, forceful remarks on everything Pierre told them.

"One used to have to be German—now one has to dance attendance on Tatáwinova and Madame Kwüdener, and wead Ecka'tshausen and the bwethwen. Oh, they should just turn that fine fellow Bonaparte loose again—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Fancy giving command of the Semyonov wegiment to a fellow like that Schwa'tz!" he cried. Tatáwinova and Krüdener were fashionable mystics of the day, and Eckartshausen a mystical writer of the same stripe.

Nicholas, though he lacked Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was a very serious, weighty matter, and it seemed to him a matter of real importance that A had been appointed Minister of This, and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such and such, and this minister had said such and such. And so he thought it his duty to take an interest in these things, and questioned Pierre closely. The questions the two of them put kept the conversation from straying beyond its ordinary character—gossip about the upper reaches of government.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had long been wanting, without managing it, to steer the conversation onto another track and give voice to the idea he felt so deeply, the very idea for whose sake he had gone to Petersburg to consult with his new friend Prince Theodore, and she came to his aid by asking how things had gone with Prince Theodore.
"What was it about?" asked Nicholas.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, glancing around at his listeners. "Everyone can see things have gotten so bad that they can't go on this way any longer, and that it's the duty of every decent man to work against it as far as he can."
"What can decent men do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What is there to be done?"
"Well, this..."
"Come into my study," said Nicholas.

Natasha, who had long expected to be sent for to nurse her baby, now heard the nurse calling her and went off to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and little Nicholas Bolkonski, unnoticed by his uncle, followed them in and sat down at the writing table, in a shadowy corner by the window.
"Well, what would you do?" asked Denisov.
"Always some fantastic scheme or other," said Nicholas.

"Why this," Pierre began, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and lisping: "the situation in Petersburg is this. The Emperor pays no attention to anything anymore. He's given himself over entirely to this mysticism"—Pierre could no longer stand mysticism in anyone—"he only wants peace, and only these people, sans foi ni loi,* can give it to him—people who go around recklessly hacking and strangling everything: Magnitsky, Arakcheev's ally, and the rest of that crowd.... You'll agree that if you didn't oversee your own estates yourself, and only wanted a quiet life, the harsher your steward was, the more easily your object would be achieved," he said to Nicholas.
* Without faith or law.
"Well, and where does that lead?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is going to ruin! Robbery in the law courts, nothing in the army but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements (colonies where soldiers were made to farm under military discipline); the people are being tormented, education is being crushed. Everything young and honest is being ground down! Everyone can see this can't go on. Everything is stretched so tight that it's bound to snap," said Pierre—much as everyone who has ever examined the actions of any government has said, since governments began. "I told them just one thing, in Petersburg."
"Told whom?"

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful glance from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the rest of them. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent—but under the present circumstances, something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew was in the room. His face darkened, and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you in here?"

"Why? Let him stay," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and going on. "That's not enough, I told them. Something else is needed. When you're standing there expecting the overstretched string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe, then as many people as possible need to join hands, as tightly as they can, to stand against the coming disaster. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One man is drawn off by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and off they go, over to that camp. There are no independent men left—men like you or me. What I'm saying is: widen the scope of our society, let the watchword be not virtue alone, but independence and action as well!"
Nicholas, who had let go of his nephew, irritably pulled up an armchair, sat down in it, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what end?" he burst out. "And what position would you take toward the government?"

"Why, the position of helpers. The society needn't be secret at all, if the government allows it. It's not just not hostile to the government—it's a society of true conservatives, a society of gentlemen in the fullest sense of the word. Its whole purpose is to stop some Pugachev or other—some peasant leader like the one behind Pugachev's rebellion—from murdering my children and yours, and to stop Arakcheev from sending me off to some Military Settlement. We join hands only for the public good and the general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society, and so a hostile one, a harmful one, one that can only do harm."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe" (they did not yet dare suggest that it was Russia that had saved Europe) "do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it's love, mutual aid... it's what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked happily at her husband. It was not what he was saying that pleased her—that did not even interest her, since to her it all seemed extremely simple, and she felt she had known it for a long time, because she knew it sprang from Pierre's whole soul—but it was his animated, enthusiastic look that made her glad.

The boy with the thin neck rising from his turned-down collar—whom everyone had forgotten about—watched Pierre with even greater and more rapturous delight. Every word Pierre spoke burned itself into his heart, and, with a nervous movement of his fingers, he found himself unconsciously breaking the sealing wax and the quill pens that came to hand on his uncle's table.
"It isn't at all what you think; but that's what the German Tugendbund was, and it's what I'm proposing."

"No, my fwiend! The Tugendbund's all vewy well for sausage eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pwonounce it," Denisov broke in, loudly and firmly. "I agwee that evewything here is wotten and howwible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If we're not satisfied, let's have a wevolt of our own. That's fine by me. Je suis vot'e homme!"*
* "I'm your man."

Pierre smiled, Natasha burst out laughing, but Nicholas only knitted his brows further, and set about proving to Pierre that there was no real prospect of any great change, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his own imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and, since his mental powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas found himself cornered. This only made him angrier still, since he was fully convinced—not by reasoning, but by something inside him stronger than reason—of the rightness of his own view.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying, with nervously twitching fingers, to prop his pipe up in a corner, then finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten, and that a collapse is coming: I don't see it. But you also say our oath of allegiance is some kind of conditional thing, and to that I say to you directly: 'You are my best friend, as you well know, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever government it may be—I know it's my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate an instant, and I'd do it.' Argue about that all you like!"

An awkward silence followed these words. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it did what she wanted. The conversation started up again, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, little Nicholas Bolkonski went up to Pierre, pale, his eyes shining and radiant.
"Uncle Pierre, you... no... If Papa were alive... would he agree with you?" he asked.

And Pierre suddenly grasped what a special, independent, complicated, and powerful process of thought and feeling must have been going on in this boy throughout the whole conversation, and, remembering everything he had said, he wished the lad had not heard him. Still, he had to give him some answer.
"Yes, I think so," he said, reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed only now to notice what he had done to the things on the table. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me, I did that... without meaning to," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
Nicholas started angrily.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the bits under the table.
And, plainly holding back his irritation with some effort, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been in here at all," he said.
